Assignment 2 — Non-Linear Regression and Regularization¶

Dataset: Concrete Compressive Strength, UCI Machine Learning Repository (I-Cheng Yeh, 1998) Task: regression. Predict the compressive strength of concrete (MPa) from its mix recipe and its age.

Why this dataset is non-linear. Concrete strength comes from chemical hydration, so it is non-linear in physically well-known ways:

  • it rises steeply in the first days and then plateaus with age (roughly logarithmic);
  • it depends on the water-to-cement ratio (Abrams' law), which is a ratio and interaction between two inputs, not an additive effect;
  • additives such as slag, fly ash and superplasticizer interact with cement and water.

A straight-line model cannot represent these effects, so this dataset is a good place to study how model complexity (polynomial degree) and regularization (Ridge and Lasso) change performance.

Requirement Section
Linear Regression evaluated with MSE, RMSE and R² 3
Polynomial features with multiple degrees, compared 4
Identifying underfitting and overfitting 5
Ridge and Lasso regularization and their impact 6
Code, comparison results, plots and conclusion 7–8, results/, figures/

The original column names are long and inconsistent (double spaces, trailing spaces), so I shorten them. The data has no missing values, but 25 rows are exact duplicates (the same mix tested at the same age). I drop them so that the same mix cannot sit in both the training and the test set, which would make test scores look better than they are. All inputs are amounts in kg per m³ of mixture, except age (days). The target strength is in MPa.

2. Is the relationship really non-linear?¶

In [5]:
features = df.columns[:-1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(15, 6.5), sharey=True)

Observations

  • age has a clearly curved effect: strength climbs fast up to about 28 days and then flattens. A straight line cannot follow that shape.
  • No single input is strongly linearly correlated with strength (the highest is cement at about 0.5). The strongest driver is the ratio of water to cement, which is curved and involves two inputs at once. A linear model in the raw features cannot form a ratio. Polynomial features add squared terms and cross terms (e.g. water·cement), which can approximate it.

Both points suggest that a linear model will underfit.

3. Baseline: Linear Regression¶

Train/test protocol. I hold out a random 20% as the test set and use it only to report final numbers. Every modelling choice (degree, α) is made with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.

Metrics.

  • MSE (mean squared error) = mean of (y − ŷ)². It is in MPa² and penalises large errors heavily. It is the quantity Linear Regression minimises.
  • RMSE = √MSE. It is in the same unit as the target (MPa), so it reads as the typical size of a prediction error.
  • R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot. It is the share of the variance in strength that the model explains. 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always predicting the mean, and a negative value is worse than predicting the mean.
In [7]:
X, y = df[features], df["strength"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=SEED)
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
print(f"train: {len(X_train)} rows | test: {len(X_test)} rows")

FITTED = {}

def evaluate(model, name, extra=None):
    """Fit on train; report train / 5-fold CV / test metrics."""
    cvs = cross_validate(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    p_tr, p_te = model.predict(X_train), model.predict(X_test)
    row = {"model": name,
           "train MSE": mean_squared_error(y_train, p_tr), "test MSE": mean_squared_error(y_test, p_te),
           "train RMSE": mean_squared_error(y_train, p_tr) ** 0.5, "CV RMSE": np.sqrt(-cvs["test_score"]).mean(),
           "test RMSE": mean_squared_error(y_test, p_te) ** 0.5,
           "train R²": r2_score(y_train, p_tr), "test R²": r2_score(y_test, p_te)}
    row.update(extra or {})
    FITTED[name] = model
    return row

linear = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("lr", LinearRegression())])
lin_row = evaluate(linear, "Linear Regression")
pd.DataFrame([lin_row]).set_index("model").round(3)

The linear model explains only about 60% of the variance, with a typical error of about 10 MPa. The residual plot shows the reason. If the model captured the true relationship, residuals would scatter randomly around 0. Instead they follow a clear arch against age. The model over-predicts very young concrete (≤ 7 days, negative residuals) and very old concrete (≥ 180 days), and under-predicts concrete in the 28–100 day range. A straight line in age cannot follow the fast-rise-then-plateau curing curve. A systematic pattern like this is the signature of a model that is too simple, i.e. underfitting (high bias).

4. Polynomial Regression: degrees 1 to 6¶

PolynomialFeatures(degree=d) adds every product of inputs up to total degree d (squares, cubes and interactions such as water·cement). The model is still linear in its coefficients, so it is solved with ordinary least squares, but it is non-linear in the original inputs.

Pipeline: PolynomialFeatures(d) → StandardScaler → LinearRegression. Scaling after the expansion keeps terms like cement³ (about 10⁸) on the same scale as age. That matters for numerical stability, and it is essential for Ridge and Lasso later, because their penalty treats every coefficient equally.

In [9]:
def poly_model(degree, reg=None):
    return Pipeline([("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False)),
                     ("scale", StandardScaler()),
                     ("reg", reg if reg is not None else LinearRegression())])

DEGREES = range(1, 7)
poly_rows = []
for d in DEGREES:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    model = poly_model(d)
    n_feat = PolynomialFeatures(d, include_bias=False).fit(X_train).n_output_features_
    poly_rows.append(evaluate(model, f"Polynomial degree {d}", {"degree": d, "n_features": n_feat,
                                                               "fit time (s)": time.perf_counter() - t0}))
poly_df = pd.DataFrame(poly_rows).set_index("model")
poly_df.to_csv(RES_DIR / "polynomial_degree_comparison.csv")
poly_df[["n_features", "train RMSE", "CV RMSE", "test RMSE", "train R²", "test R²", "train MSE", "test MSE"]].round(3)

5. Identifying underfitting and overfitting¶

Degree Features Pattern Diagnosis
1 8 train and test error both high (RMSE about 10 MPa) and close to each other Underfitting (high bias). The model is too simple to represent the curvature and interactions.
2 44 both errors fall a lot, small gap better, still somewhat biased
3 164 lowest CV and test error, moderate gap best bias-variance balance without regularization
4 494 train error keeps falling, test error jumps (test R² < 0) Overfitting (high variance). With 494 parameters for about 800 rows, the model memorises noise.
5–6 1,286–3,002 more features than training rows. Train R² is about 1, test R² is hugely negative severe overfitting. Predictions outside the training points are meaningless.

How to tell them apart:

  • Underfitting: training error itself is high, and train ≈ test. More data will not help, but more model capacity will.
  • Overfitting: training error is low but validation/test error is much higher. The gap between them is the warning sign. Fixes are more data, less capacity, or regularization.

The plots above also show the classic U-shape of the validation error. Training error always decreases as complexity grows, so it cannot be used to choose the degree. That is why the degree is chosen by cross-validation.

6. Regularization: Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1)¶

Regularization keeps the flexible feature set but adds a penalty on coefficient size to the least-squares loss:

$$\textbf{Ridge:}\ \min_w \ \|y - Xw\|^2 + \alpha\|w\|_2^2 \qquad\qquad \textbf{Lasso:}\ \min_w\ \tfrac{1}{2n}\|y - Xw\|^2 + \alpha\|w\|_1$$

  • α controls the strength. α → 0 recovers plain least squares (overfit), and a very large α forces all coefficients toward 0 (underfit). Somewhere in between is the best trade-off, chosen by cross-validation.
  • Ridge shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero but never exactly to zero. It is especially good with many correlated features, such as polynomial terms.
  • Lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero, so it also performs automatic feature selection and gives a sparser, more interpretable model.

I regularize the degree-4 model, the first one that clearly overfits (494 features, test R² < 0), and ask whether the penalty can turn its extra flexibility into better generalization.

For each α I compute the 5-fold CV RMSE on the training set. The polynomial expansion and scaler are refitted inside every fold so nothing leaks. The α with the lowest CV error is selected, and only then is the test set used.

In [12]:
REG_DEGREE = 4
RIDGE_ALPHAS = np.logspace(-4, 3, 36)
LASSO_ALPHAS = np.logspace(0.5, -3, 36)          # lasso_path expects a decreasing sequence

def prep(X_fit, *others):
    """Fit polynomial expansion + scaler on X_fit only, transform the others with it."""
    pipe = Pipeline([("poly", PolynomialFeatures(REG_DEGREE, include_bias=False)), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    out = [pipe.fit_transform(X_fit)] + [pipe.transform(o) for o in others]
    return out, pipe

def ridge_curve(Xa, ya, Xb, yb):
    tr, te = [], []
    for a in RIDGE_ALPHAS:
        m = Ridge(alpha=a).fit(Xa, ya)
        tr.append(mean_squared_error(ya, m.predict(Xa)) ** 0.5); te.append(mean_squared_error(yb, m.predict(Xb)) ** 0.5)
    return np.array(tr), np.array(te)

def lasso_curve(Xa, ya, Xb, yb):
    """Whole regularization path in one call (warm starts make this fast)."""
    ym = ya.mean()
    _, coefs, _ = lasso_path(Xa, ya - ym, alphas=LASSO_ALPHAS, max_iter=50_000, tol=1e-4)
    tr = np.sqrt(((Xa @ coefs + ym - ya.values[:, None]) ** 2).mean(axis=0))
    te = np.sqrt(((Xb @ coefs + ym - yb.values[:, None]) ** 2).mean(axis=0))
    return tr, te, coefs

t0 = time.perf_counter()
cv_ridge, cv_lasso = [], []
for tr_idx, va_idx in cv.split(X_train):
    Xa, ya, Xb, yb = X_train.iloc[tr_idx], y_train.iloc[tr_idx], X_train.iloc[va_idx], y_train.iloc[va_idx]
    (Xa_t, Xb_t), _ = prep(Xa, Xb)
    cv_ridge.append(ridge_curve(Xa_t, ya, Xb_t, yb)[1])
    cv_lasso.append(lasso_curve(Xa_t, ya, Xb_t, yb)[1])
cv_ridge, cv_lasso = np.mean(cv_ridge, axis=0), np.mean(cv_lasso, axis=0)

(Xtr_t, Xte_t), poly4 = prep(X_train, X_test)
ridge_tr, ridge_te = ridge_curve(Xtr_t, y_train, Xte_t, y_test)
lasso_tr, lasso_te, lasso_coefs = lasso_curve(Xtr_t, y_train, Xte_t, y_test)
best_ridge_alpha = RIDGE_ALPHAS[np.argmin(cv_ridge)]
best_lasso_alpha = LASSO_ALPHAS[np.argmin(cv_lasso)]
print(f"done in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f}s")
print(f"best Ridge α = {best_ridge_alpha:.4g} (CV RMSE {cv_ridge.min():.3f})")
print(f"best Lasso α = {best_lasso_alpha:.4g} (CV RMSE {cv_lasso.min():.3f})")

done in 137s
best Ridge α = 0.2512 (CV RMSE 5.936)
best Lasso α = 0.001995 (CV RMSE 5.755)

for ax, alphas, tr, cvv, te, best, name in [
        (axes[0], RIDGE_ALPHAS, ridge_tr, cv_ridge, ridge_te, best_ridge_alpha, "Ridge (L2)"),
        (axes[1], LASSO_ALPHAS, lasso_tr, cv_lasso, lasso_te, best_lasso_alpha, "Lasso (L1)")]:
    ax.plot(alphas, tr, color=PALETTE[0], label="train RMSE")
    ax.plot(alphas, cvv, color=PALETTE[1], label="5-fold CV RMSE")
    ax.plot(alphas, te, color=PALETTE[2], label="test RMSE")
    ax.axvline(best, color=MUTED, lw=1)
    ax.text(best * 1.15, 14.2, f"CV-selected α = {best:.3g}", color=INK2, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("α (regularization strength, log scale)")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}, degree-{REG_DEGREE} features"); ax.set_ylim(3, 16)
axes[0].set_ylabel("RMSE (MPa)"); axes[1].legend(loc="center left")
for ax, lo, hi in [(axes[0], RIDGE_ALPHAS.min(), RIDGE_ALPHAS.max()), (axes[1], LASSO_ALPHAS.min(), LASSO_ALPHAS.max())]:
    ax.text(lo * 1.3, 15.3, "← overfit (weak penalty)", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.text(hi / 1.3, 15.3, "underfit (strong penalty) →", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5, ha="right")
fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "06_regularization_alpha_curves")

For reference, the unregularized degree-4 model has a test RMSE of 39.2 MPa, far above the top of these charts.

Each panel shows the same story as the degree plot, but with α as the complexity control reversed:

  • Small α (left) is close to unregularized least squares: very low training error and high validation error, i.e. overfitting.
  • Large α (right) penalises so hard that the model collapses toward predicting the mean: both errors rise together, i.e. underfitting.
  • The CV-selected α sits at the bottom of the validation U-curve. Train, CV and test errors then sit close together, which means the model generalizes.

max |coef| L2 norm of coefs non-zero coefs
Degree 4, no regularization 12504.45 53922.67 494

Degree 4 + Lasso (α=0.002) 58.94 163.47 161

The table shows why the unregularized degree-4 model fails. To fit the training noise it uses huge coefficients that cancel each other out (look at the L2 norm). Those cancellations fall apart on new data, which is what high variance looks like in practice. Ridge shrinks the coefficient vector by orders of magnitude. Lasso does the same and also discards most of the 494 terms.

Which terms does Lasso keep?

The largest surviving terms are dominated by age (age⁴, age³ and their interactions with the mix components), which model the curved, saturating hardening curve. Next come interactions between cement, water and the aggregates, the mix-proportion effects described by Abrams' law. Individual high-order coefficients should not be over-interpreted, because polynomial terms are strongly correlated with each other. The set of selected terms is the informative part.

8. Conclusion¶

Model Features (non-zero) Train R² Test R² Test RMSE (MPa) Diagnosis
Linear Regression 8 0.61 0.58 11.19 underfitting (high bias)
Polynomial degree 2 44 0.81 0.77 8.31 still somewhat biased
Polynomial degree 3 164 0.93 0.88 5.94 best unregularized model
Polynomial degree 4 494 0.98 −4.15 39.19 severe overfitting (high variance)
Degree 4 + Ridge (α = 0.25) 494 0.93 0.89 5.71 well-regularized
Degree 4 + Lasso (α = 0.002) 494 (161) 0.94 0.89 5.67 well-regularized and sparse
  1. Linear Regression underfits. It explains only about 60% of the variance (test RMSE 11.2 MPa), and its residuals follow a systematic arch against age. Concrete strength is genuinely non-linear in its inputs.
  2. Polynomial features fix the bias, up to a point. Degree 2 and degree 3 cut the test error almost in half (R² 0.58 → 0.88). From degree 4 onward the model overfits: training R² keeps rising to about 0.99, while test R² collapses below zero, i.e. worse than predicting the mean. The widening train–test gap and the U-shaped validation curve are the signatures used to tell underfitting from overfitting.
  3. Regularization rescues the overfit model. On the same 494 degree-4 features, Ridge and Lasso (α chosen by cross-validation) bring test R² from −4.15 to 0.89, which also beats the best unregularized model (degree 3). The penalty shrinks the coefficients from a maximum of about 12,500 (huge values cancelling each other out) to a few dozen, so the model keeps the flexibility of degree 4 without memorising noise.
  4. Ridge vs Lasso. Their accuracy is practically tied (test RMSE 5.71 vs 5.67 MPa, well within noise). The difference is in the model they produce. Ridge keeps all 494 terms with small weights; it is fast and stable with correlated features. Lasso sets two thirds of the coefficients exactly to zero (161 of 494 kept), which gives a sparser, more interpretable model. Lasso had the lowest CV error and is my recommended model, with Ridge an equally valid choice when simplicity of fitting matters.

Take-away: model complexity should be chosen by validation error, never by training error. A flexible model plus well-tuned regularization usually generalizes better than a model whose capacity is restricted by hand. A natural next step would be physically motivated features (log-age, water/cement ratio) or tree ensembles, which handle such non-linearities without manual polynomial expansion.
